question: How does memory allocation work in C++?

scenes.sub: Three kinds of storage, and who is responsible for each.
scenes.say: How does memory allocation work in C plus plus? Every object gets one of three kinds of storage. Let's watch all three in one small program.

scenes.head: Three kinds of storage
scenes.say: A global like counter has static storage. It exists for the whole run of the program. Inside f, the local x lives on the stack, created automatically when f is called. But new int of forty two is different. It asks the heap for memory at runtime, and p stores its address. Delete p hands that memory back. When f returns, x and p vanish automatically. Heap memory never does. It stays until someone frees it.

scenes.head: Where heap memory comes from
scenes.say: So where does heap memory come from? Your code writes new. That calls a function named operator new, which on GCC and Clang usually just calls malloc. The allocator keeps lists of free blocks and hands out one big enough. Only when it runs out does it ask the operating system for more pages. That bookkeeping, and the occasional system call, is why the heap is slower than the stack.

scenes.head: Modern C++: let an owner allocate

panels.code:
int scores[10];                       // stack: automatic

std::vector<int> big(1'000'000);      // heap, owned by big
auto w = std::make_unique<Widget>();  // heap, owned by w

Widget* raw = new Widget;             // heap, owned by... you
delete raw;                           // forget this: leak

scenes.say: In modern C plus plus, you rarely call new yourself. Small, short lived data goes on the stack. For heap memory, use an owner, like a vector, or make unique. The owner frees the memory automatically when it goes out of scope. Raw new and delete still work, but every new needs exactly one delete, on every path. That's where leaks and crashes come from.

lines: Three storage kinds: static (whole program), automatic (stack), dynamic (heap).
new → operator new → allocator (usually malloc) → OS pages when it runs out.
Prefer the stack and owning types (vector, unique_ptr) over raw new/delete.
scenes.say: Three kinds of storage: static for the whole program, automatic on the stack, and dynamic on the heap. Heap memory flows from new, to operator new, to the allocator, and from the operating system when needed. Prefer the stack, and owning types like vector and unique pointer, over raw new and delete.
